title: uXMS, uQueryDB, and uPokeDB
prompt: What is the practical difference between using uXMS, uQueryDB, and uPokeDB when debugging a MOOS variable during a mission?

chatgpt.text:
The practical difference is:

uXMS = “watch variables live.”
Use it when you want to see whether a variable is being posted, what its current value is, and whether it is changing.

Example:

Bash
uXMS targ_shoreside.moos DEPLOY MOOS_MANUAL_OVERRIDE RETURN NAV_X NAV_Y

Good for asking:

Is DEPLOY actually true?
Is NAV_X updating?
Did my app ever post VISIT_POINT?
Is MOOS_MANUAL_OVERRIDE stuck true?

It is usually the first debugging tool to reach for during a running mission.

uQueryDB = “ask the MOOSDB for the current value once.”
Use it when you want a quick snapshot of one or more variables without opening a live terminal view.

Example:

Bash
uQueryDB targ_alpha.moos DEPLOY

or:

Bash
uQueryDB targ_alpha.moos NAV_X NAV_Y

Good for scripts, quick checks, or when you just want to know:

What is the current value right now?
Does the MOOSDB currently know this variable?

Compared to uXMS, it is less useful for watching timing, repeated posts, or changing values.

uPokeDB = “manually post/set a variable.”
Use it when you want to inject a value into the MOOSDB to test whether the rest of the mission reacts correctly.

Example:

Bash
uPokeDB targ_alpha.moos DEPLOY=true MOOS_MANUAL_OVERRIDE=false

or:

Bash
uPokeDB targ_alpha.moos RETURN=true

Good for asking:

If I manually set DEPLOY=true, does the helm start?
If I poke RETURN=true, does the behavior react?
Is the problem upstream, because no one is posting the variable, or downstream, because the behavior ignores it?

This is not just observation; it changes mission state.

A clean mental model:

uXMS      = watch
uQueryDB  = ask once
uPokeDB   = force/post

For debugging a variable like DEPLOY, I would usually do:

Bash
uXMS targ_alpha.moos DEPLOY MOOS_MANUAL_OVERRIDE IVPHELM_STATE

Then, if DEPLOY is missing or false:

Bash
uPokeDB targ_alpha.moos DEPLOY=true MOOS_MANUAL_OVERRIDE=false

Then watch again in uXMS to see whether IVPHELM_STATE, behavior activity, or vehicle motion changes.

The big caution: uPokeDB can mask the real bug. If poking DEPLOY=true fixes the mission, that does not mean the mission is configured correctly. It means the downstream behavior works, but your launch script, action button, uTimerScript, or app that was supposed to post DEPLOY may still be broken.

Claude responded: These three tools sit at different points in the debug workflow and give you different kinds of access to MOOS variables:

These three tools sit at different points in the debug workflow and give you different kinds of access to MOOS variables:

uXMS is your live, interactive dashboard. It subscribes to the MOOSDB in real time and displays a continuously updating table of variable names, their current values, timestamps, and who published them. You use this when you want to watch one or more variables evolve as the mission runs — it's the go-to for "what is this variable doing right now?" It requires the community to be running.

uPokeDB is for writing to the MOOSDB — you're pushing a value into a variable from the command line. This is useful for injecting test values, forcing a state change, or simulating a sensor reading without the actual hardware. Think of it as a one-shot "set this variable to this value" tool. It connects, pokes the variable, and exits.

uQueryDB is for reading a snapshot from the command line without launching a full GUI. It connects to a running MOOSDB, fetches the current value of one or more variables, prints them, and exits. It's handy in scripts or when you just want a quick one-time check rather than an ongoing watch.

Practical workflow analogy:

Scenario	Tool
"I want to watch NAV_SPEED evolve during the mission"	uXMS
"I want to check what DEPLOY is set to right now in a script"	uQueryDB
"I want to manually trigger a behavior by setting MOOS_MANUAL_OVERRIDE=false"	uPokeDB

The key distinction is directionality and interactivity: uXMS is a sustained, interactive read; uQueryDB is a one-shot read; uPokeDB is a one-shot write. During a real debug session you'd typically use uXMS to observe the symptom, uPokeDB to poke a hypothesis ("what if I force this variable?"), and uQueryDB in any automated test scripts checking postconditions.

gemini.text:
When debugging an autonomous vehicle mission running on the MOOS (Mission Oriented Operating Suite) middleware, you frequently need to interact with the central database (MOOSDB).

While uXMS, uQueryDB, and uPokeDB all act as lightweight command-line MOOS clients, they serve fundamentally different operational purposes: uXMS is for observation, uPokeDB is for active intervention, and uQueryDB is for automated conditional checking.

The practical differences come down to how they interact with MOOS variables during a mission:

1. uXMS: The Live Observer (Scoping)

uXMS is a terminal-based tool used purely for monitoring (scoping) the state of your variables in real-time. It acts like a live sensor readout of the MOOSDB.

Behavior: It connects to the MOOSDB, subscribes to the variables you specify, and dynamically refreshes the terminal screen with their current values, update frequencies, and which app last wrote to them (source/auxiliary source).

Best Used For: * Verifying that a variable is changing as expected (e.g., checking if NAV_DEPTH is fluctuating).

Debugging behavior conflicts by watching the "auxiliary source" column to see exactly which IvP Helm behavior is writing to a control variable.

Key Constraint: It is strictly passive; you cannot alter data using uXMS.

2. uPokeDB: The Direct Intervener (Poking)

uPokeDB is a "fire-and-forget" command-line utility used to manually force or inject a value into a MOOS variable.

Behavior: When executed from the terminal, it connects to the MOOSDB, displays the targeted variable’s current value, overwrites ("pokes") it with your new designated value, verifies the change took place, and immediately disconnects/terminates.

Best Used For: * Manually overriding states during a live simulation or field test (e.g., forcing a deployment by running uPokeDB DEPLOY=true alpha.moos).

Simulating sensor failures or specific edge-case inputs to see how the autonomy system handles them.

Key Constraint: It is an instantaneous, one-time operation. If another app (like a simulator or sensor driver) is publishing to that same variable at a high frequency, your poked value will be instantly overwritten.

3. uQueryDB: The Automated Gatekeeper (Testing)

uQueryDB is a command-line tool designed to evaluate a logical condition against the database and instantly close out, returning a standard Linux exit code (0 for true, 1 for false).

Behavior: It connects to the MOOSDB, registers for the variables in your logical condition, waits for the data to arrive, evaluates the statement, and exits immediately. You can use the --wait=N flag to give it a timeout window to wait for a condition to become true.

Best Used For: * Automating simulation testing via bash scripts (e.g., waiting for a vehicle to return home before shutting down the simulation: uQueryDB alpha.moos --condition="NAV_X < 10").

Checking termination criteria or safety boundaries in automated test suites.  
MIT Marine Autonomy Lab

Key Constraint: It does not give a continuous live view like uXMS, nor does it alter any data like uPokeDB. It simply checks a fact and leaves.

Quick Comparison Summary
Tool	Primary Action	Lifespan	Typical Command Example
uXMS	Watch variables continuously.	Persistent (runs until closed)	uXMS alpha.moos DEPLOY NAV_SPEED
uPokeDB	Change a variable value once.	Instantaneous (runs, pokes, exits)	uPokeDB DEPLOY=true alpha.moos
uQueryDB	Test a logical condition.	Ephemeral (exits once condition is met/fails)	uQueryDB alpha.moos --condition="SPEED > 2.0"
